title: General Sample Spaces
notes: Open by naming the change in scale: the chapter is no longer only about circles and spheres. The observations may be rotations, frames, subspaces, hyperboloid points, or manifold points, so the first statistical decision is to identify the sample space before computing a summary.

title: Lecture Route
notes: Use the route slide as a discipline for the whole lecture. Each step prevents a familiar mistake: treating a constrained object as an ordinary vector, forgetting an invariance, or fitting a model whose statistic changes when the same observation is represented in another valid way.

title: Sample-Space Inventory
notes: This slide separates the main object types. The point is not that every example needs a different computational library; it is that each example carries a different identity check, and those checks decide whether a proposed average, score, or test is meaningful.

title: Rotations
notes: Present rotations as complete oriented frames. The matrix has nine entries, but the statistical object lives on a three-dimensional curved group cut out by orthogonality and determinant constraints. This is why the matrix Fisher score sees the whole oriented frame.

title: Stiefel Frames
notes: Move from rotations to partial frames. A Stiefel point keeps only r orthonormal columns, so the data retain directional order inside the frame. Polar or QR projection is useful computationally because it repairs a noisy full-rank matrix back onto the constraint set.

title: Grassmann Projections
notes: Stress the difference between a chosen basis and the subspace it spans. The projection matrix is the coordinate-free record of the subspace, so replacing X by XQ should not change the answer. This is the practical reason Grassmann data route through P equals X X transpose.

title: Fisher Or Bingham
notes: Use the two score curves to make model routing visible. The frame score changes when the internal basis rotates, so it is appropriate only when the basis is observed. The projection score stays flat, which is exactly the behavior wanted for subspace or axial data.

title: Hyperboloid Data
notes: The hyperboloid example breaks the habit of using the Euclidean dot product everywhere. Points satisfy an indefinite quadratic identity, and the relevant symmetry preserves the Minkowski bilinear form. Also note that a full hyperboloid is noncompact, so a finite uniform model is not available.

title: Manifold Habit
notes: General manifold data do not require a single universal algorithm, but they do require a repeatable contract. Before averaging or testing, record membership, tangent or chart information, metric or geodesic structure, and the group action or quotient that should leave the scientific answer unchanged.

title: Invariant Checks
notes: Turn the geometry into executable checks. These identities are not cosmetic tests; they are the evidence that an array still represents the intended sample space after numerical construction, perturbation, projection, or model fitting. When a check fails, the statistical interpretation should pause before the estimator is interpreted.

title: Classify Before Computing
notes: This checklist is the applied workflow for new data. Students should be able to say what the observation is, what constraint defines membership, what transformations leave it unchanged, and which canonical statistic survives those transformations before any estimation routine is trusted.

title: Canonical Statistics
notes: The table compresses the chapter into a routing rule. Rotations and frames keep ordered columns, so the statistic can use the matrix itself. Subspaces and axes forget the basis, hyperboloid data use Minkowski products, and general manifolds need local or geodesic summaries.

title: One Data Pipeline
notes: Use the pipeline as a worked design pattern rather than a numerical example. A recorded object first passes a membership audit, then the invariance is stated, then the statistic is selected, and only afterward does the model score or inference step become interpretable.

title: Notebook Artifacts
notes: Connect the lecture to the notebook without relying on copied figures. The generated artifacts are useful because they expose the constraints, show the Fisher-versus-Bingham routing decision, and save JSON checks that a reader can inspect independently.

title: Pitfalls
notes: Use the pitfalls slide as a quality-control pass. Most errors in this chapter come from losing an invariance: flattening a curved space too early, keeping a basis that should have been quotiented out, or using a compact-space intuition on a noncompact sample space.

title: Recap
notes: Close by making the final prompt concrete. Given a new directional data set, the learner should classify the sample space first, state the invariant, name the canonical statistic, and attach a check that proves the computation stayed on the intended geometry.
